account: Nigeria had no urban social registry, so its National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office built the Rapid Response Register for a government-funded COVID-19 cash transfer. Berkeley and Columbia researchers, with World Bank economists, produced ward-level poverty maps by applying machine-learning algorithms to satellite imagery with household-survey labels. Using the maps, the government selected 1,163 of the poorest urban wards, with a population of over 20 million. Human Rights Watch reported in July 2021 that the program began in January 2021 as a pilot paying 5,000 naira a month to over 3,100 households in Ikorodu and Karshi. The PNAS authors state that disbursement began in mid-January 2021. Residents of the selected wards self-registered through USSD, a text menu on mobile phones, after text-message blasts whose first wave went out in June 2021. In-person verification followed. Human Rights Watch researchers argued in July 2021 that the targeting methods made it very likely that large numbers of people in need were excluded. World Bank monitoring reports 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 October 2021 in the government's COVID-19 cash transfer. The World Bank's appraisal document of November 2021 reports over 1.75 million registrations against a government target of one million households. The World Bank's status report of 29 January 2025 counts over 5 million households supported by the direct benefit transfer program, without breaking out the share that the register targeted.

ai_role.statement: Decisive at the geographic stage: the ML poverty map alone chose which 1,163 wards were eligible. Individual inclusion depended on USSD self-registration and in-person verification, not AI. Payment and registration counts come from World Bank operational documents, not from the map developers. The PNAS paper and World Bank blog are co-authored by the developers.

fields.account: Nigeria had no urban social registry, so its National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office built the Rapid Response Register for a government-funded COVID-19 cash transfer. Berkeley and Columbia researchers, with World Bank economists, produced ward-level poverty maps by applying machine-learning algorithms to satellite imagery with household-survey labels. Using the maps, the government selected 1,163 of the poorest urban wards, with a population of over 20 million. Human Rights Watch reported in July 2021 that the program began in January 2021 as a pilot paying 5,000 naira a month to over 3,100 households in Ikorodu and Karshi. The PNAS authors state that disbursement began in mid-January 2021. Residents of the selected wards self-registered through USSD, a text menu on mobile phones, after text-message blasts whose first wave went out in June 2021. In-person verification followed. Human Rights Watch researchers argued in July 2021 that the targeting methods made it very likely that large numbers of people in need were excluded. World Bank monitoring reports 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 October 2021 in the government's COVID-19 cash transfer. The World Bank's appraisal document of November 2021 reports over 1.75 million registrations against a government target of one million households. The World Bank's status report of 29 January 2025 counts over 5 million households supported by the direct benefit transfer program, without breaking out the share that the register targeted.

purpose: Geographically target a COVID-19 urban cash transfer to the poorest wards where no social registry existed.

ratings.reason: Households in selected wards were beneficiaries of the government's COVID-19 cash transfer. The PNAS authors say that disbursement began in mid-January 2021. The World Bank's status report records 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 October 2021 without saying how many had been paid.

The National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office stood up an urban registry within months through self-registration by mobile phone in the wards selected with the poverty map. The World Bank's appraisal document of November 2021 reports over 1.75 million registrations.

The sources report that the 1,163 selected wards, with over 20 million residents, were made eligible, and the 61.7% cut in inclusion errors is a simulation estimate. No source reports a realized change across that population.
